_about: Hand-curated fire-safety attributes for each PSI combustion investigation. Scores are 0-1. Every key finding cites its source; PSI metadata (objectives, DOI, dates) and test statistics are merged in by backend/spark/pipeline/build.py.

_sources.guide: NASA, A Researcher's Guide to ISS Combustion Science (NP-2015-10-034-JSC, 2015)
_sources.grc: NASA Glenn Research Center investigation fact sheets (nasa.gov Combustion Science archive)
_sources.acme: NASA Glenn, Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) overview
_sources.psi: NASA Physical Sciences Informatics investigation record

investigations.sample: 41 samples: thin flat strips 12 cm x 1-2 cm, thick PMMA 5 x 1 cm, PMMA spheres 1-2 cm, candles in 6 mm ceramic tubes
investigations.relevance: Real spacecraft materials burned in ventilation-speed airflow, then extinguished with nitrogen: the closest small-scale analogue to a cabin fire and its suppression.

key_findings.text: Materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth, so the NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 upward-burning screen is not conservative.
A local nitrogen jet can strengthen a flame: it entrains surrounding air and sustains burning even with the cabin airflow off.
Unlike on Earth, the best point to apply a suppressant to a microgravity flame is not obvious; a poorly aimed stream can feed the flame oxygen.

investigations.earth_applications: Validated flame-spread models for building and wildland fire codes.

investigations.sample: ~100 samples: flat 10 cm x 1-2 cm, rods 1/4-1/2 inch, large acrylic spherical section
measurements: O2, CO2 and CO sensors (CSA-CP, CDM)
investigations.relevance: Measured how low oxygen and airflow can go before common plastics and fabrics stop burning in microgravity: the flammability-limit data needed to pick cabin materials.

key_findings.text: Thin- and thick-fuel flame spread rates were measured in microgravity and a formula for the thin-to-thick transition was derived.
Models predict higher spread rates than observed, so flame-spread models need improvement before they can replace tests.
Oxygen was lowered below air by nitrogen vitiation (data reach ~14 % O2) to find minimum oxygen and flow limits for burning.

investigations.earth_applications: Fire models for wildfires, building fires and waste-to-energy combustion.

investigations.sample: 0.4 m x 0.94 m fabric sheet in a 0.5 x 1 x 1.3 m flow duct inside a departed Cygnus
investigations.relevance: The first fire of realistic size in space: shows how fast a large fire grows inside a spacecraft-sized volume.

key_findings.text: Before Saffire, the largest fire experiment in space was about the size of an index card.
Concurrent-flow burn of the large sample lasted ~420 s, while the opposed-flow sample burned ~70 s at the same 20 cm/s airflow.

investigations.earth_applications: Fire growth data for confined vehicles such as aircraft cabins and submarines.

investigations.sample: 9 samples, 5 cm x 29 cm, several thicknesses
investigations.relevance: Burned nine real spacecraft materials and compared the burn in microgravity with the same samples in normal gravity: direct evidence for material selection.

key_findings.text: The kit expanded beyond fabric to Nomex, silicone and the acrylic used in spacecraft windows.
The experimental table records both microgravity burn length and 1-g burn length per sample, a direct gravity comparison.

investigations.earth_applications: Material flammability rankings for transport interiors.

investigations.sample: 0.41 m x 0.94 m fabric sheet, concurrent and opposed flow
investigations.relevance: Repeated the Saffire-I fabric at a higher 30 cm/s airflow to show how ventilation speed changes large-fire growth.

key_findings.text: Same SIBAL fabric as Saffire-I but at a higher flow velocity, isolating the effect of ventilation on fire growth.

investigations.earth_applications: Ventilation-driven fire growth in confined spaces.

investigations.sample: 30 samples (6 each of 5 materials) heated to produce smoke, not flame
investigations.relevance: Measured what smoke from overheating spacecraft materials actually looks like in microgravity, the signal every smoke detector must catch.

key_findings.text: Mean smoke particle diameters were 100-200 nm, yet a large share of the mass is in particles above 1 um (silicone: AMD 227 nm with almost half the mass above 1000 nm).
Sub-micron smoke is better detected by ionization detectors, though light-scattering detectors would work for most cases.
Detectors should target pre-fire overheating (pyrolysis) products, not soot, because spacecraft cannot tolerate established flaming fires.

investigations.earth_applications: Smoke detection for submarines and underwater habitats.

investigations.sample: Heated material samples on a wick/heater, with smoke aged in a chamber
investigations.relevance: Re-flight that tested whether existing spacecraft smoke detectors see the smoke that real cabin materials make in microgravity.

key_findings.text: ISS smoke detectors use near-IR forward scattering and are most sensitive to particles above 1 um, outside the Shuttle detector's range.
Skylab's ~30 UV fire detectors were line-of-sight only and suffered false alarms.
Six component failures by overheating occurred in the Shuttle fleet; none became a fire, but longer missions raise the odds.

investigations.earth_applications: Detector designs that reject nuisance alarms.

investigations.sample: Ambient ISS air and a dust aerosol; no combustion
measurements: Modified TSI P-Trak ultrafine particle counter
investigations.relevance: Characterized normal ISS dust so detectors can tell harmless dust from smoke, and proved the particle counter used later in SAME.

key_findings.text: ISS particulate levels were low compared with the Shuttle, and average particle sizes were larger on orbit than on Earth.
Knowing background dust levels helps design detectors that distinguish dust from smoke (fewer false alarms).

investigations.earth_applications: Dust-versus-smoke discrimination, as in NASA's incipient fire detector used in mining.

investigations.sample: Free or fiber-supported droplets 2-5 mm in a quiescent chamber
investigations.relevance: Quantified how much CO2 or helium it takes to put out a fire in microgravity: the basis for gaseous suppression in spacecraft.

key_findings.text: The limiting oxygen index is lower in reduced gravity than on Earth, so terrestrial inert-gas suppressant standards do not offer the same margin of safety in space.
Large heptane droplets kept burning as an invisible low-temperature 'cool flame' after the visible flame went out, a discovery first doubted by peers.
Suppressants studied were CO2 and helium, at reduced pressure too, because venting a cabin is one way to fight fire.

investigations.earth_applications: Validated chemistry models for liquid fuels used in engines; suppressant design.

investigations.sample: Single droplets and droplet pairs, 1.5-5 mm, some in slow forced flow
investigations.relevance: Extended FLEX to practical fuels, slow airflow and interacting droplets, closer to a real spill or spray fire.

key_findings.text: Studied sooting, sub-buoyant convective flow and droplet-droplet interactions with pure, mixed and surrogate fuels.
Sooting propensity changes with the inert diluent at the same oxygen level.

investigations.earth_applications: Fuel spray models for engines and biofuels.

investigations.sample: Free and fiber-supported droplets
investigations.relevance: Maps when low-temperature cool flames appear across 0.5-5 atm, a burning mode that conventional detectors and suppression logic do not expect.

key_findings.text: Examined cool-flame burning of dodecane droplets at pressures from 0.25 to 5 atm.

investigations.earth_applications: Cool-flame chemistry for cleaner, more efficient engines.

investigations.sample: Porous spherical burner; normal flames (fuel out) and inverse flames (oxygen out)
investigations.relevance: Contains the highest oxygen concentrations tested in microgravity (up to 85 % O2 in inverse flames), the closest data to oxygen-enriched lunar habitats and EVA prep.

key_findings.text: Inverse flames issued oxygen-nitrogen mixtures of up to 85 % O2 into a fuel-laden chamber: the highest-oxygen microgravity combustion tests in PSI.
Cool diffusion flames were observed as steady spherical flames for the first time.

investigations.earth_applications: Cool-flame kinetics for engine design.

investigations.sample: Porous spherical burner, normal and inverse flames, oxygen-enriched atmospheres
investigations.relevance: Mapped when flames start to make soot in oxygen-enriched air up to 85 % O2; soot drives flame radiation and smoke.

key_findings.text: Tests whether the stoichiometric mixture fraction can characterize soot and flammability limits of non-premixed flames, as equivalence ratio does for premixed flames.

investigations.earth_applications: Cleaner, soot-free burner design.

investigations.sample: Flat porous burner (25-50 mm) whose fuel flow mimics a burning solid's vaporization
investigations.relevance: Purpose-built for spacecraft fire prevention: emulates burning materials at 21-40 % O2 in still air to judge flammability tests for low and partial gravity.

key_findings.text: Unlike the other ACME experiments, BRE targets fire prevention: it assesses existing flammability tests for low- and partial-gravity environments.
Flames were ignited at oxygen levels of 21, 25, 26.5, 34 and 40 %, spanning air to lunar-habitat-like enrichment.

investigations.earth_applications: Material property-based fire hazard ranking.

investigations.sample: Coflow burner, fuel dilution varied from pure (sooty) to near-extinction
investigations.relevance: Shows that microgravity flames are far sootier than on Earth, which changes radiation and the smoke a detector sees.

key_findings.text: Microgravity sooty flames are taller, wider, cooler and contain 5-8 times more soot than equivalent normal-gravity flames.
Highly diluted weak flames are more stable in microgravity, so flames survive at lower fuel concentrations than on Earth.

investigations.earth_applications: Soot models for engines and climate studies.

investigations.sample: Coflow or gas-jet flame with a high-voltage mesh (up to +/-10 kV) downstream
investigations.relevance: Electric fields push on flame ions to create an 'ion wind', a way to mimic partial-gravity buoyancy without leaving the ISS.

key_findings.text: Partial gravity was mimicked through the electric field's effect on the ions that naturally occur in flames.
Electric fields can modify flame shape, alter soot or flammability limits and direct heat transfer.

investigations.earth_applications: Electric flame control for low-emission combustion.

investigations.sample: Porous spherical burner, flames left to extinguish naturally
investigations.relevance: Pins down both radiative and convective extinction limits, the physics behind when a fire goes out on its own.

key_findings.text: Aims to identify extinction limits for both radiative and convective extinction and the onset of pulsating instabilities.

investigations.earth_applications: Validated flame models.

investigations.sample: Gas-jet flames from 3 nozzles in a fan-driven duct
investigations.relevance: Soot controls how much heat a fire radiates and how much smoke it makes; SPICE measured when microgravity flames start to smoke.

key_findings.text: Over 70 smoke points were identified, giving soot-forming conditions and flame sizes in microgravity.
Soot dominates the heat emitted by flames in normal and microgravity fires; controlling it matters for fire spread.
Results let heat-release data from the NASA cone calorimeter be extended to microgravity for performance-based material selection.

investigations.earth_applications: Smoke-point data used in terrestrial fire modeling.

investigations.sample: Coflow jet flames in the SPICE duct, air speed raised until liftoff
investigations.relevance: Flame attachment to a surface controls whether a fire stays anchored, relevant to how airflow can blow out or relocate a flame.

key_findings.text: Flame attachment to (or detachment from) a burner or condensed-fuel surface is essential to fire safety; the attachment point controls stability of the whole flame.

investigations.earth_applications: Burner stability and emissions.

investigations.sample: Re-analysis of SPICE images with color-ratio pyrometry
investigations.relevance: Explains why soot differs so much between 1 g and 0 g flames, supporting fire detection and suppression models.

key_findings.text: Combined flight imaging and detailed soot models to explain the 1-g vs 0-g soot discrepancy.

investigations.earth_applications: Soot prediction tools.

investigations.sample: Computational model validated with two-color tomography
investigations.relevance: A predictive model of flame spread over solids in microgravity, built and checked against BASS data.

key_findings.text: Developed and validated flamelet-generated-manifold models for concurrent flame spread, one of the hardest cases to model.

investigations.earth_applications: Faster fire-spread simulation.

investigations.sample: Direct numerical simulation of smoke particle growth
investigations.relevance: Simulates how gravity changes smoke particle growth, so detector designs can be tested virtually.

key_findings.text: Simulated smoke particle formation and growth in Earth gravity and microgravity from SAME conditions.

investigations.earth_applications: Smoke transport modeling.

investigations.sample: 3-D OpenFOAM model of droplet cool flames
investigations.relevance: Shows how small thermal and airflow disturbances change cool-flame behavior, using FLEX flight data.

key_findings.text: Quantified how imposed thermal and convective perturbations affect droplet cool-flame dynamics.

investigations.earth_applications: Engine combustion modeling.

investigations.sample: Counterflow flame experiments and three kinetic models
investigations.relevance: Explains how oxygen level sets the extinction limits of cool flames observed in FLEX.

key_findings.text: Compared oxygen-concentration effects on cool-flame extinction limits with three numerical models using FLEX conditions.

investigations.earth_applications: Low-temperature combustion chemistry.
